directions.opening: **A mass-spring system can vibrate in two directions, and both directions work the same way.** In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves back and forth along the spring. In **transverse motion**, the mass moves up and down across the system, between stretched supports.
directions.mechanism: When the mass moves away from **equilibrium** (its resting position), a **restoring force** pulls it back. Because of **inertia**, the moving mass keeps going past equilibrium, so it overshoots and gets pulled back again. In the transverse system, the **tension** (pulling force) in the stretched supports supplies the restoring force.
directions.consequence: So only the direction of the motion changes between the two systems. **The restoring force and the overshoot stay the same.**

mass-stiffness.opening: **In a mass-spring system, more mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises it.** **Frequency** (pitch) is the number of complete cycles in one second. Each rule holds only when the other property stays the same.
mass-stiffness.mechanism: More mass is harder to speed up and turn around, so each cycle takes longer. A stiffer spring pulls back harder for the same stretch, so the mass returns more quickly.
mass-stiffness.consequence: So a prediction has to say which property changed and which one stayed the same. If mass and stiffness both change, you have to weigh both effects together.

economy.opening: **A dynamical model describes how something changes over time, and it can describe an economy as well as a spring.** In an economic model, the variables are economic states, not the position of a block. The model can show a quantity moving back toward an **equilibrium** (a stable level).
economy.mechanism: **Feedback** is the effect a change has back on itself. Depending on how the parts connect, feedback can shrink a change or make it grow. So a change in one part can affect the later behavior of the whole system.
economy.consequence: So the economy and the spring share **the way change is organized over time**. They do not share the same physical material.

notes_v10_1: - **A mass-spring system vibrates because the spring keeps pulling the mass back, and the moving mass keeps going past the middle.** A **mass-spring system** is a mass attached to a spring. The spring has a resting length, called its **equilibrium position**.
- The spring always pulls or pushes toward its equilibrium position. If the spring is stretched, it pulls. If the spring is compressed, it pushes.
- A moving mass keeps moving until something stops it. It does not stop by itself.
- In short, the spring "wants" to rest, and the moving mass "wants" to keep going.
- **The vibration happens in four steps that repeat.**
- First, the mass is pulled out and let go, and the stretched spring pulls the mass back toward the middle.
- Second, the mass reaches the middle while it is still moving, so it keeps going and compresses the spring.
- Third, the compressed spring pushes the mass back the other way.
- Fourth, the mass passes the middle again and stretches the spring, and the cycle starts over. This repeating back and forth is called **vibration**.
- **Friction is left out of the model.** On a real table, friction slowly stops the motion. In the model there is no friction, so the mass vibrates forever.
- **The same system can move in two directions.** Both directions follow the same rules, but some systems are easier to understand in one direction than the other.
- Longitudinal motion: The mass moves **left and right**, along the line of the spring.
- Transverse motion: The mass sits between **two walls** with one spring on each side, and the mass moves **up and down**, across the line of the springs.
- **Longitudinal motion and transverse motion work in exactly the same way.** In transverse motion, pulling the mass up stretches both springs, and the stretched springs pull the mass back down.
- When the mass passes the middle, the springs are not stretched. The mass is still moving, so it keeps going and stretches the springs on the other side.
- Both versions vibrate at the **same rate**, because they have the same mass and the same total stiffness in the direction the mass moves.

title: Modes: how a system with many masses vibrates

two-modes.opening: **Two masses joined by springs have two normal modes, and Mode 2 is faster.** A **normal mode** is one organized pattern of motion of the whole system. In **Mode 1**, the two masses move together. In **Mode 2**, they move in opposite directions.
two-modes.mechanism: When the masses move together, the middle spring is hardly stretched. When they move in opposite directions, the middle spring and the outer springs all stretch. So the restoring force is stronger and **the frequency is higher**.
two-modes.consequence: So a mode is a pattern of the whole system, not a frequency that belongs to one mass. Both masses take part in each mode, and the two modes can combine into more complicated motion.

three-modes.opening: **Three masses joined by springs have three normal modes, ordered from the lowest to the highest frequency.** In **Mode 1**, all three masses move together in one broad motion. In **Mode 2**, the middle mass stays still. In **Mode 3**, each mass moves opposite to its neighbor.
three-modes.mechanism: In Mode 2, the two outer masses move in opposite directions, so their pulls on the middle mass balance and it does not move. In Mode 3, the direction switches between every pair of neighbors. So the springs stretch the most, and Mode 3 has the highest frequency.
three-modes.consequence: So extra mass on the middle mass **lowers Mode 1 and Mode 3**, where that mass moves. It **does not change Mode 2**, because the middle mass sits at a **node** (a spot that does not move) in the ideal symmetric system.

many-modes.opening: **A system with N masses that can each move on their own has N normal modes.** This holds when the masses move in only one direction. Each added mass allows one more pattern of vibration.
many-modes.mechanism: The lower modes have broad patterns, and the higher modes switch direction more often along the system. The system does not have to pick one mode, because it can vibrate in several modes at once.
many-modes.consequence: So with a huge number of tiny masses and springs, the system becomes a **string**. A string has a whole series of modes, and their spacing also depends on its shape and on how its ends are held.

notes_v10_1: - **Two masses can vibrate in two different ways, and each way is called a mode.** The system has two walls, one spring from each wall to a mass, and **one spring between the two masses**. All the masses are equal, and all the springs have the same stiffness.
- A **mode** is a way of vibrating. The modes are told apart by one question, which is whether the masses move together or against each other.

- **In Mode 1, the masses move together.** Both masses are pulled up and let go, and they rise and fall side by side. In longitudinal motion, both masses are pulled to the left, and they move left and right as a pair.

- **In Mode 2, the masses move against each other.** One mass is pulled down and the other mass is pulled up. After they are let go, one mass rises whenever the other mass falls. In longitudinal motion, the masses move toward each other and then apart.
- **A system can also vibrate in both modes at the same time.** To start this mixed motion, both masses are pulled up, but one mass is pulled higher than the other.
- Both masses fall together, which is Mode 1.
- The masses start at different heights, so the middle spring also pushes them against each other, which is Mode 2.
- So the masses move together and against each other at once. Real movement and real speech production do this all the time.
- **Mode 2 has a higher frequency than Mode 1.** When the masses move together, they go back and forth slowly. When the masses move against each other, they go back and forth quickly.
- **The reason is how many springs are actually stretching.** Both modes use the same two masses and the same three springs, so the answer comes from checking what each spring does.
- In both modes, the **two outer springs** stretch and compress.
- Mode 1: The masses move together, so the **middle spring never stretches or compresses**. The middle spring moves with the masses like a solid bar, so **Mode 1 effectively has only two springs**.

- Mode 2: The masses move against each other, so the middle spring is stretched and compressed again and again. **All three springs are working**, so Mode 2 has three units of stiffness instead of two.

- **More working stiffness gives a stronger pull back to the middle, and a stronger pull gives a higher frequency.** The springs themselves did not change. Only the way each mode uses the springs changed.
- The general rule is that **the more the masses move against each other, the more the springs stretch, so the higher the frequency**.
- A higher mode does not have stiffer springs. A higher mode makes the same springs do more stretching.
notes_v9_3: - A system with **two masses** has two walls, one spring from each wall to a mass, and **one spring between the two masses**. All the masses are equal, and all the springs are equally stiff. This system can vibrate in **two different ways**, which are called **modes**. **A mode is simply one way that a system can vibrate.**
- In **Mode 1**, the masses move **together**. If you pull both masses up and let go, they rise and fall side by side. In longitudinal motion, they move left and right as a pair.
- In **Mode 2**, the masses move **against each other**. If you pull one mass down and the other up, then whenever one rises, the other falls.
- In longitudinal motion, Mode 2 means one mass is pulled left and the other right, so they move toward each other and then apart.

- A system can also vibrate in **both modes at the same time**. If you pull both masses up, but one higher than the other, they move together and against each other at once. Real movements, including speech, do this all the time.

- **When the masses move together, they go back and forth slowly. When they move against each other, they go back and forth quickly.** So **Mode 2 has the higher frequency**. Both modes use the same masses and the same springs, so to explain the difference, look at **what each spring is doing**.
- In **Mode 1**, the middle spring never stretches or compresses. It just rides along like a solid bar, so **Mode 1 really only uses two springs**.
- In **Mode 2**, the middle spring is stretched and squished over and over. So **all three springs are working**, and Mode 2 has three springs' worth of stiffness instead of two.

- **More stiffness means a stronger pull back toward equilibrium, and a stronger pull means a higher frequency.** In plain terms, a higher mode does not use stiffer springs. It makes the same springs do more stretching.

- This leads to a general rule. **The more the masses move against each other, the more the springs stretch and compress. That gives the mode more stiffness, so it has a higher frequency.** This is why a system with several masses has several frequencies. It has several modes, and each higher mode is stiffer than the one before it.

notes_v10_1: - **Two masses have two modes, and Mode 2 is faster because more springs are stretching.** In **Mode 1**, the masses move together. In **Mode 2**, the masses move against each other. The system can also do both at once.
- Mode 1: The middle spring moves with the masses without stretching, so effectively Mode 1 has **only two springs**.
- Mode 2: All **three springs** stretch and compress. More working springs give **more stiffness** and a **higher frequency**.
- **A spring only matters in a mode where that spring stretches.** Suppose the **middle spring is made stiffer** while the system vibrates.
- **Mode 1 does not change**, because the middle spring never stretches in Mode 1.
- **Mode 2 gets faster**, because the middle spring stretches and compresses all the time in Mode 2.
notes_v9_3: - A system with **two masses** has **two modes**. In **Mode 1**, the masses move together. In **Mode 2**, they move against each other. The system can also do both at once.
- **Mode 1 is slower**, because the middle spring just rides along without stretching. So in practice, Mode 1 uses **only two springs**.
- **Mode 2 is faster**, because all **three springs** stretch and compress. More working springs means **more stiffness**, and more stiffness means a **higher frequency**.

- Suppose you make the **middle spring stiffer** while the system vibrates. **Mode 1 does not change**, because the middle spring never stretches in Mode 1. **Mode 2 goes up**, because in Mode 2 the middle spring is always stretching and compressing.
- In plain terms, a spring only matters in a mode where it is being stretched.
- The system can also vibrate in **both modes at once**. The masses rise and fall together while also moving against each other, which is how real systems usually move.

notes_v10_1: - **Each of the three modes has its own frequency, from lowest to highest.** The system has three masses and four springs.
- Mode 1: All three masses move **together**. Mode 1 has the **lowest frequency**.

- Mode 2: The **middle mass stays still** while the two outer masses move against each other. Mode 2 has the **middle frequency**. To start Mode 2, the outer masses are pulled apart without touching the middle mass.
- Mode 3: The **middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses**. Mode 3 has the **highest frequency**. In transverse motion, the middle mass goes down while both outer masses go up.
- **The frequencies follow the same stiffness rule.**
- Mode 1 is slow because the masses move together, so the **two middle springs do not stretch**, and springs that do not stretch add no stiffness.
- In Mode 2, the springs stretch and compress, but less than they could.
- In Mode 3, **every mass moves against its neighbor**, so the springs stretch the most. Mode 3 has the most stiffness and the fastest motion.
- **Changing one mass only affects the modes where that mass moves.** A mass changes frequency only by moving.
- Making the **middle mass heavier lowers the frequency of Mode 1 and Mode 3**, because the middle mass moves in both of those modes.
- The same change leaves **Mode 2 the same**, because the middle mass does not move in Mode 2.
- **All three modes can happen at the same time.** However the system is started, the system vibrates as some mix of these **pure modes**.

- Learning a musical instrument means learning to make the masses and springs vibrate in some modes and not others. How a string is plucked or a violin is bowed decides which modes start, and those modes are heard as **notes**.
- A **trained singer** does the same thing with the vocal folds, controlling their mass and stiffness to sing in tune.
notes_v9_3: - With **three masses** and four springs, the system has **three modes**, and each mode has its own frequency.
- In **Mode 1**, all three masses move back and forth **together**. This mode has the **lowest frequency**, because the two middle springs just ride along and add no stiffness.

- In **Mode 2**, the **middle mass stays still** while the two outer masses move against each other. This mode has the **middle frequency**. To start it, you pull the outer masses apart carefully without touching the middle one.

- In **Mode 3**, the **middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses**, so **every mass moves against its neighbors**. This mode has the most stretching and compressing, the most stiffness, and the **highest frequency**.

If you make the **middle mass heavier**, the frequency of **Mode 1 and Mode 3 goes down**, because the middle mass moves in both of those modes. **Mode 2 does not change**, because the middle mass does not move at all in Mode 2.

- **Learning a musical instrument means learning how to make its masses and springs vibrate in certain modes and not others.** How you pluck a string or bow a violin decides which modes start vibrating, and the strongest modes are what we hear as **notes**.
- A **trained singer** does the same thing with the vocal folds. The singer controls the mass and stiffness of the folds well enough to sing in tune.

In Mode 2, the middle mass stays still while the two outer masses move against each other. In Mode 3, the middle mass moves against both outer masses.

- **Mode 3 gets slower**, because Mass 2 moves in Mode 3.

notes_v10_1: - **Every added mass adds one more mode, so N masses give N modes.** One mass has one mode, two masses have two modes, and six masses have six modes.
- Higher modes have more **reversals**. A reversal is a place where two neighboring masses move in opposite directions.
- More reversals mean more stretching, so **higher modes have higher frequencies**.
- In a chain of separate masses like this, the mode frequencies are usually **not whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency.
- **The same mode has the same pattern in every chain, no matter how many masses the chain has.**
- **Mode 1** always has all the masses moving up and down together.
- **Mode 2** always has the **left side moving against the right side**. With an odd number of masses, the middle mass stays still.
- **Mode 3** always has the **middle moving against the two sides**.
- With **four masses**, the four modes are all four together, the left pair against the right pair, the middle pair against the outer pair, and every mass against its neighbors.

- **A chain with an infinite number of masses and springs is a string**, like a guitar string or a piano string. Every small piece of a string has mass, and every small piece stretches like a spring, so a string has an infinite number of modes.
- In the **lowest mode**, the whole string moves up and down together with almost no stretching, and this mode gives the **lowest note**.
- In each higher mode, more parts of the string move against each other.
- A string plucked without skill vibrates in many modes at once.

Higher modes have **more reversals**, which are places where neighboring masses move in opposite directions. More reversals mean more stretching, so **higher modes have higher frequencies**.
- In a chain of separate masses like this, the mode frequencies are usually **not whole-number multiples** of the lowest frequency.

- A **building** is like a string that is fixed to the ground at the bottom and free to sway at the top. Engineers design buildings to sway only in **Mode 1**, because in higher modes some floors would move one way while other floors moved the other way.

title: Membranes, complex vibrations and testing the theory

membrane.opening: **A membrane is a stretched sheet, so it can vibrate in patterns across a whole surface, not just along a line.** Different parts can move together or in opposite directions. Several of these patterns can be present in one overall motion.
membrane.mechanism: A measurement at one point picks up every mode that moves at that point. A **spectrum** (a graph of how strong each frequency is) separates those modes by frequency, even when the motion looks messy.
membrane.consequence: So a spectrum can pull apart a complicated membrane vibration. The evenly spaced frequencies in the membrane demonstration are teaching values, so **not every real membrane has evenly spaced modes**.

scientific-method.opening: **A theory can be tested when it makes a prediction you can measure.** The theory that the vocal folds vibrate as a membrane predicts **evenly spaced harmonics** in a recorded voice. **Harmonics** are the peaks in the spectrum of a repeating sound.
scientific-method.mechanism: The prediction links the proposed mechanism to a pattern you can see. Recording a voice and checking its spectrum tests whether the peaks have the expected spacing. So you accept the theory because the measurement matches, not because it sounds right.
scientific-method.consequence: So a good test connects the theory, the predicted spectrum and the measurement. A matching result supports the prediction, but **it does not prove every part of the theory**.

title: Fixed-fixed and fixed-free systems: harmonics and formants

fixed-fixed.opening: **A uniform string fixed at both ends must have a node at each end, because neither end can move.** A **node** is a spot that does not move. **Mode 1** fits one half-wave between the ends, and the next modes fit two, three and more half-waves.
fixed-fixed.mechanism: Fitting more half-waves into the same length makes each wave shorter. The wave speed stays the same, so shorter waves have higher frequencies. That is why the modes are **whole-number multiples** of Mode 1, called the **harmonics**.
fixed-fixed.consequence: So if Mode 1 is 200 Hz, **Mode 5 is 1,000 Hz**. A spectrum up to Mode 6 has peaks at 200, 400, 600, 800, 1,000 and 1,200 Hz, with frequency on the horizontal axis.

fixed-free.opening: **A fixed-free system has one fixed end and one free end, so its two ends behave differently.** The fixed end cannot move, so it is a node. The free end moves the most.
fixed-free.mechanism: One **quarter-wave** goes from a still point to a point of greatest motion. To keep the free end moving the most, the next mode adds two more quarter-waves. That gives 1, 3, 5 and 7 quarter-waves.
fixed-free.consequence: So the modes are **odd multiples** of the lowest one, at 1, 3, 5 and 7 times. The air in a neutral vocal tract is fixed at the closed glottis and free at the open lips. A building is also fixed at one end and free at the other, at the ground and at the top.

notes_v10_1: - **A string fixed at both ends has modes at whole-number multiples of its lowest frequency.** If the lowest mode is at **100 hertz**, the next modes are at **200, 300, 400 and 500 hertz**. **Hertz** means times per second. Modes that line up as whole-number multiples are called **harmonics**.
- **The even spacing comes from counting copies of the first mode.** **Mode 1 is one bump.** **Mode 2 is two copies of that bump**, with one half going up while the other half goes down.
- Two copies give Mode 2 **twice the stiffness** of Mode 1, so Mode 2 has twice the frequency.
- Mode 3 holds three copies and has three times the frequency. The fifth mode holds **five copies of the first mode**, so it has five times the frequency.
- So each mode adds one more unit of stiffness, and the frequencies climb in equal steps. If the lowest mode is 200 hertz, the fifth mode is five times 200.
- **A real string vibrates in all of its modes at the same time.** The separate motions add together into one complicated shape, and that combined shape is what a plucked string actually does.
- **A spectrum shows which frequencies are in a sound and how strong each one is.** **Frequency** runs along the horizontal axis, and **amplitude**, which is strength, runs up the vertical axis.

- For a string vibrating in all five modes, the spectrum has **five evenly spaced spikes**, one spike at each mode's frequency. In this example the spikes have **equal height**, because nothing has filtered the sound.

- If the string vibrated **only in Mode 3**, the spectrum would have **one spike at the frequency of Mode 3** and nothing else. A list with one active slot and every other slot at zero is called a **one-hot encoding**.

title: Where the springiness is, and what a local change does

local-change.opening: **In a vibrating system, a change at one spot affects each mode according to what that spot does in that mode.** Extra mass matters where the mode moves. Extra stiffness matters where the mode stretches or compresses.
local-change.mechanism: Where a mode moves the most, the extra mass has the biggest effect, so **the frequency goes down**. At a node, the spot does not move but is stretched the most. So extra stiffness **raises the frequency**, with no mass effect working against it.
local-change.consequence: So one spot can be a node in one mode and a point of greatest motion in another. Adding mass and stiffness there can raise one mode and lower the other, so **the two changes do not cancel**.

notes_v10_1: - **All of these results come from a short list of principles about masses and springs.** The principles connect to each other, so they do not need to be memorized as separate facts.
- **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency.**
- **A system with n masses has n modes of vibration**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency.
- **Adding mass lowers the frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves.** How much the mass moves depends on where the mass is.
- **Where there is the most movement there is no stretching, and where there is the most stretching there is no movement.**
- **Adding stiffness raises the frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses.** This also depends on where the spring is.
- In a **fixed-fixed system**, the harmonics are **whole-number multiples of the base frequency**, because the first mode fits a whole number of times into each mode.
- In a **fixed-free system**, the frequencies are **odd multiples of the base frequency**, because the first mode fits an odd number of times into each mode.
notes_v9_3: - All of the results so far come from a short list of **principles of mass-spring systems**, and they all fit together.
- **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency.**
- **A system with n masses has n modes of vibration**, and each higher mode has a higher frequency.
- **Adding mass at a spot lowers the frequency more when that spot moves more.** How much a spot moves depends on where it is.
- **Where there is the most movement, there is no stretching. Where there is the most stretching, there is no movement.**
- **Adding stiffness at a spot raises the frequency more when that spot stretches and compresses more.** This also depends on where the spot is.

- In a **fixed-fixed system**, which is fixed at both ends, the harmonics are **whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency**, because each mode holds a whole number of copies of the lowest mode. In a **fixed-free system**, which is fixed at one end and free at the other, they are **odd multiples**, because each mode holds an odd number of copies.

notes_v10_1: - **One small change to a string can make one mode lower and another mode higher.** Choose a spot where **Mode 4 moves the most** and where **Mode 5 crosses its middle line**, so Mode 5 does not move at that spot. Then raise both the **mass** and the **stiffness** of that spot.
- **For Mode 4**, the spot is moving, so the extra mass **lowers** the frequency. The spot is barely stretched, so the extra stiffness does nothing.
- **For Mode 5**, the spot does not move, so the extra mass does nothing. The spot is stretched the most, so the extra stiffness **raises** the frequency.
- So the same change **lowers Mode 4 and raises Mode 5**.

- **Each mode is checked separately with one question, which is whether the spot is moving or stretching in that mode.** If the spot is moving, the mass is what matters. If the spot is stretching, the stiffness is what matters.

- **This reasoning about small local changes is called perturbation theory, and it was first tested on drums.** A drum is also made of countless masses and springs. In the late nineteenth century, before cameras could record fast motion, small amounts of **wax** were stuck onto different spots on a drum.
- Wax on a spot predicted to vibrate a lot added moving mass, and listeners heard the drum's frequency **drop**.
- Wax on a spot predicted not to move made **no difference** to the sound.
notes_v9_3: - Changing one small piece of a string can push two modes in **opposite directions**. Take a spot where **Mode 4 moves the most** and where **Mode 5 crosses its middle line**, so Mode 5 does not move there at all. Now add both **mass** and **stiffness** to that piece.
- **For Mode 4**, the piece is moving, so the extra mass **lowers** the frequency. The piece is barely stretched, so the extra stiffness does nothing.
- **For Mode 5**, the piece does not move, so the extra mass does nothing. The piece is stretched the most, so the extra stiffness **raises** the frequency.
- So the same change **lowers Mode 4's frequency and raises Mode 5's frequency**. Work out each mode separately by asking whether the spot is moving or stretching in that mode.

- **Perturbation theory** predicts how a small change in one location affects how something vibrates. In the late nineteenth century, researchers tested this by placing small amounts of **wax** on different parts of a **drum**.
- When wax was placed where the drum vibrated a lot, the extra mass made the drum vibrate more slowly, causing its frequency (pitch) to **decrease**.
- When wax was placed where the drum did not vibrate, it had **no effect** on the drum's frequency or sound.

notes_v10_1: - **The mass-spring principles explain every vowel.** Raising mass lowers frequency, and raising stiffness raises frequency, but each change only matters where it can act.
- **Extra mass matters where the air moves.**
- **Extra stiffness matters where the air compresses and expands.**
- The vocal tract is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips, so its formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one.
notes_v9_3: - The same principles explain all the vowels. **Extra mass matters where the air moves, and extra stiffness matters where the air compresses and expands.** The vocal tract is fixed at the glottis and free at the lips, so its formants are **odd multiples** of the lowest one.

notes_v10_1: - **Every vibrating system in speech follows the same short list of principles.**
- **Raising the mass lowers the frequency, and raising the stiffness raises the frequency.**
- **A system with n masses has n modes.** Each higher mode has a higher frequency, because more parts move against each other and more springs stretch.

- **Adding mass lowers the frequency in proportion to how much that mass moves.** A mass that does not move has no effect. A mass that moves a little has a small effect. A mass that moves a lot has a large effect.
- **Adding stiffness raises the frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches and compresses.** Both effects depend on where the change is made.
- **Where there is the most movement there is no stretching, and where there is the most stretching there is no movement.**
- In a **fixed-fixed system**, the frequencies are called **harmonics**, and they are **whole-number multiples** of the base frequency.
- In a **fixed-free system**, the frequencies are called **formants**, and they are **odd multiples** of the base frequency.

- **Raising mass and stiffness at the same time does not cancel out, except for a single mass on a single spring.** In a system with many masses and springs, a spot that moves a lot hardly stretches, and a spot that stretches a lot hardly moves. So at any one spot, only one of the two changes matters.

- Picture a spot on a string that moves up and down the most. Extra stiffness at that spot does nothing. Extra mass at that spot slows it down. So the frequency goes down.

In a system with many masses and springs, a spot that moves a lot is hardly stretching, and a spot that stretches a lot is hardly moving. So at any one spot, only one of the two changes matters.

title: Air in the vocal tract: moving versus compressed

air-modes.opening: **The air in the vocal tract moves longitudinally, back and forth along the tube from the glottis to the lips.** The wave-shaped curve in the diagram shows how far the air moves at each spot. The air does not travel up and down inside the mouth.
air-modes.mechanism: Where neighboring bits of air move toward each other, the air is **compressed** and the pressure rises. Where they move apart, the air spreads out. So how much the air moves and how much it is compressed are two different things.
air-modes.consequence: So near a node, the air hardly moves but is **strongly compressed**. Near the spot of greatest motion, the air moves a lot but is hardly compressed. That is why a constriction has different effects in different places.

notes_v10_1: - **The air in the vocal tract can be modeled as a chain of masses and springs that is fixed at the glottis end and free at the lip end.** In this model, the masses stand for the air's inertia, which is its resistance to being moved, and the springs stand for its springiness.
- The lowest mode of the chain is like the **first formant**, written **F1**. The next mode is like the **second formant**, written **F2**.
- The frequencies of a fixed-free system are called **formants**. The frequencies of a fixed-fixed system are called **harmonics**.
- The second mode vibrates **three times faster** than the first, because the second mode holds three quarter-wave pieces.
- The masses near the free end move very freely in both modes.
- **Three places along the tube matter for vowels.**
- /a/: The constriction is **one-third of the way from the glottis**.
- /i/: The constriction is **two-thirds of the way from the glottis**.
- /u/: The constriction is at the **lips**, which is the free end.

notes_v10_1: - **A constriction raises both the stiffness and the mass of the air.**
- Stiffness: Compressed air becomes **stiffer**, the same way pressing on a tire makes the tire stiffer.
- Mass: A constriction also packs the air into a smaller space, which raises its **density**. Denser air is more **massive** and harder to move.
- **Raising mass and stiffness together does not cancel out in a system with many masses and springs.** Canceling out only happens for a single mass on a single spring.
- In a system with many masses and springs, each spot is either mostly **moving** or mostly **stretching** in a given mode.
- At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, only the extra stiffness counts, so the frequency **goes up**.
- At a spot with lots of motion and no stretching, only the extra mass counts, so the frequency **goes down**.
- Speech proves that the effects do not cancel, because constrictions in different places clearly change the frequencies of the voice.
notes_v9_3: - **Squeezing air raises both its stiffness and its mass.** Squeezed air is like the air in a tire, which gets **stiffer** when it is squeezed. Packing air into a smaller space also raises its **density**, which makes it more **massive**.

- You might think that raising mass and stiffness together would **cancel out**. **That is false** for any system with many masses and springs, because in a given mode each spot is either mostly **moving** or mostly **stretching**.
- At a spot with no motion and lots of stretching, only the extra stiffness counts, so the frequency **rises**.
- At a spot with lots of motion and no stretching, only the extra mass counts, so the frequency **falls**.
- Speech itself proves the effects do not cancel, because constrictions in different places clearly change the frequencies of the voice.

title: Source and filter, F0 and high voices

source.opening: **In the source-filter model, the vocal folds are the source, and they make a harmonic series.** The lowest harmonic is the **fundamental frequency**, F0. The other harmonics fall at whole-number multiples of F0.
source.mechanism: A faster repeating source spaces the harmonics farther apart. Stiffer vocal folds tend to **raise F0**, and more vibrating mass in the folds tends to **lower F0**.
source.consequence: So at an F0 of 150 Hz, the first five harmonics are 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz. These numbers describe the source, and the tract decides how strong each one is.

filter.opening: **In the source-filter model, the vocal tract is the filter, and it changes how strong each harmonic is.** It strengthens frequencies near its resonances, which are called **formants**. **F1** and **F2** are the first two formants.
filter.mechanism: Harmonics close to a formant stay strong, and harmonics far from any formant get weaker. The outline of the harmonic heights is the **envelope**, and its broad peaks show the shape of the tract.
filter.consequence: So changing the vowel can move the formants while **F0** (the fundamental frequency of the voice) stays the same. Changing F0 changes the spacing of the harmonics while the tract shape stays about the same. So **pitch and vowel are separate**.

sparse-harmonics.opening: **A high F0 spreads the harmonics far apart, so fewer of them fall near each formant.** A formant can then sit between two harmonics. No nearby peaks are left to show its shape.
sparse-harmonics.mechanism: A low voice has many closely spaced harmonics around each formant, so the envelope is easy to see. A high voice has only a few, so the envelope is **hard to estimate** from the spectrum.
sparse-harmonics.consequence: So vowels can be hard to identify in very high singing or high-pitched speech. **The tract still has its formants**, and a formant does not turn into the fundamental.

notes_v10_1: - **The vocal folds are the source, and their mass and stiffness set F0 and the spacing of the harmonics.**
- **Big, heavy, loose vocal folds** have a large mass and a small stiffness, so their **F0 is low**, around 100 hertz, with harmonics at 200, 300 and so on.
- **Tighter, lighter vocal folds** have a higher F0, such as 250 hertz, with harmonics at 500 and 750 hertz.
- **Very tight, light vocal folds** have an even higher F0, such as 350 hertz, with harmonics at 700 and 1050 hertz.

- **F0 keeps changing while people talk.** Only a robot keeps F0 constant. Speakers change F0 by tightening and loosening the vocal folds with the muscles in the larynx, and listeners use those changes to understand meaning.
- When **"The dog slept here"** is a statement, F0 falls at the very end. When the same words are a question, F0 rises at the end.
- The way F0 moves also tells listeners whether a person is being sarcastic, pretending, or even lying.

- **F0 can be measured in Praat.** Take a short piece of speech, view a spectral slice, and pick the lowest harmonic. One measured voice had F0 around 170 hertz, and the next harmonic was at about twice that value, as the theory predicts.

vowel-network.opening: **The vowel network takes F1 and F2 as its two inputs and gives a probability for each of five words.** The five outputs stand for done, dune, dean, Don and Dan. Each output position belongs to one word.
vowel-network.mechanism: The hidden layers turn the two formants into new numbers that the last layer uses. The learned **weights** decide which formant patterns support which word.
vowel-network.consequence: So a low F1 with a high F2 matches /i/, and **the right answer for that input is dean**. Getting it right depends on learning how formants relate to words, not on memorizing the order of the recordings.

network-shape.opening: **The vowel network has 2 inputs, three hidden layers and 5 output neurons.** The hidden layers have 3, 2 and 4 neurons, in that order. The 2 inputs are F1 and F2, and the 5 outputs are the five words.
network-shape.mechanism: Every layer is **fully connected**, so each neuron gets one weight from every neuron in the layer before it. So the number of weights into one neuron depends on the size of the layer before, not on the number of outputs.
network-shape.consequence: So the input layer only supplies F1 and F2 and does no processing. That leaves **four processing layers**, which match the four Linear lines in the program.

weights.opening: **In a neural network, a weight controls how much an incoming activation adds to the next neuron.** The receiving neuron multiplies each input by its weight. Then it adds up the results, which gives the **weighted sum**, also called the **inner product**.
weights.mechanism: A positive weight keeps the sign of the input, and a negative weight flips it. The size of the weight sets how strong the contribution is, so **a large weight is not automatically a good one**.
weights.consequence: So random starting weights have not learned the vowels yet. Training improves the network by changing the weights in response to its errors.

forward.opening: **Forward propagation is how a network makes a prediction with its current weights.** Each processing layer combines the activations from the layer before. Its results become the inputs to the next layer.
forward.mechanism: The input layer only supplies the measured values, so it has no weights of its own. The output layer turns the final numbers into the network's decision among the possible words.
forward.consequence: So a network can finish a forward pass correctly and **still make the wrong decision**. Making a prediction and improving the weights are separate jobs, but the prediction is needed to find the error.

probabilities.opening: **A probability distribution is a list of numbers that are never negative and add up to 1.** The output of the vowel network is one such list. Each number is the chance the network gives to one word.
probabilities.mechanism: The position of each number tells you which word it belongs to. The **target** (desired output) for dean puts 1 in the dean position and 0 everywhere else. That gives training a specific answer to aim for.
probabilities.consequence: So **a valid distribution can still favor the wrong word**. Validity checks the form of the output, and accuracy checks whether the favored word matches the recording.

backward.opening: **Backpropagation is how a network works out how each weight should change, and it starts at the output.** The error is most directly tied to the last processing layer. sigmoid-flow.opening: **When the sigmoid changes a hidden value, every later layer changes too.** The later layers take that hidden value as their input. So the rest of the network has to be recalculated, not just one number replaced.
sigmoid-flow.mechanism: Each hidden neuron first adds up its weighted inputs, and then it applies the sigmoid. The output of the sigmoid is the value that travels along the outgoing connections.

overlap.opening: **When the vowel recordings are plotted by F1 and F2, the vowel categories overlap.** Each point is one recording, placed by its two formant values. So one pair of formants does not always point to just one vowel.
overlap.mechanism: Nearby points have similar formants even when they are different vowels. So the network must learn useful boundaries from the labeled examples. It cannot expect each vowel to have its own separate region.
overlap.consequence: So the plot shows how hard the problem is before training is judged. **Accuracy on the training data** does not by itself show how well the network does on new speakers.

accuracy.opening: **Accuracy is the share of decisions the network gets right.** With five equally likely words, random guessing is right one time in five. So **chance accuracy is 20 percent**.
accuracy.mechanism: Accuracy can rise as the weights learn useful differences, though the curve may jump around before it settles. When it levels off, more updates in that run are no longer improving the training decisions.
accuracy.consequence: So this linear network's run **levels off near 45 percent** on its training data. That result describes this network and this run, not a limit for all neural networks or vowel classifiers.

initialization.opening: **Different starting weights can lead to different learning paths on the same data.** The starting weights are random. They change the early predictions and gradients, even when the network and the training steps stay the same.
initialization.mechanism: The ten runs shown take different routes but reach **the same final training accuracy**. So the path can vary while the end result stays the same.
initialization.consequence: So repeated runs give stronger evidence about this training setup than one chosen run. Their agreement does not promise the exact same number with every software library or every starting point.

notes_v10_1: - **The real formant data from the class shows why AI is hard.** Each recording is a dot. **F1** is on the horizontal axis, and **F2** is on the vertical axis. There are 525 dots, 105 for each vowel.

- The data also has **a lot of overlap**. Many /æ/ dots sit among the /i/ dots, and many others overlap with schwa. The /u/, /a/ and schwa groups pile on top of each other.

title: From one neuron to sequences: recurrent networks and LLMs

brain-model.opening: **A model neuron is a math version of a real neuron that links incoming activity, connection strengths and one output.** It simplifies what a real neuron does into steps that can be calculated and studied.
brain-model.mechanism: The weights stand for how strongly each incoming signal counts. The weighted sum captures one part of how a neuron gathers information. It leaves out the chemical and electrical details of a real neuron.
brain-model.consequence: So the model is useful for the behavior it helps explain. Borrowing the idea from biology **does not make a network the same as a brain**.

recurrent.opening: **A recurrent network sends its own output back into part of its input, so each step depends on the one before.** A regular network classifies one static vector at a time. A recurrent network carries information from one moment to the next.
recurrent.mechanism: Michael Jordan invented the recurrent network in 1985 to model **speech production**, how the tongue, velum and lips move during speech. Speech production and prediction both depend on information that unfolds over time. The feedback gives the next step its context.
recurrent.consequence: So the network keeps transforming its information while holding on to **the context it needs**. GPT also feeds each new word back in, though modern language models add other mechanisms besides recurrence.

levels.opening: **AI systems are built in levels, from a neuron to a network to an LLM to an agentic system.** A neuron combines its inputs into one number. A network combines layers of neurons, and an LLM uses context to predict what comes next.
levels.mechanism: An **agentic system** connects LLMs through messages and assigned tasks. So one LLM's output can become another LLM's input. These connections sit outside the hidden layers of any single model.
levels.consequence: So the same weighted sums stay useful as the system grows more complex. **Adding a higher level does not make the lower-level computations disappear.**

next-token.opening: **An LLM is given a sequence of vectors and predicts the next one, whatever the vectors stand for.** A **vector** is a list of numbers. Words, sounds, images and other data can all be turned into vectors. For example, the model can be given 15 vectors and asked to predict the 16th.
next-token.mechanism: The model uses the context so far to give a probability to each possible next item. When the real next item arrives, it gives feedback, so learning improves those probabilities.
next-token.consequence: So the position and context of each item help decide what should come next. **The task stays the same** whether the vectors are words, sounds or amino acids.

It learns its weights by making mistakes and correcting them with **backpropagation**.
- **The idea began in 1943 with a paper by McCulloch and Pitts.** The paper proposed that simple math could model how the brain works.
- The paper starts from the **all-or-none** behavior of neurons. All means active, and none means inactive, so a neuron is either firing or not firing.
- All-or-none is the same idea as the **sigmoid**. So the very first paper on artificial neural networks started from biology, from how real neurons behave.
- Warren McCulloch was a **psychiatrist**. The earliest work on neural networks tried to model how the mind works, including mental illness, and was not about making money.
- **By 1986, the ideas had grown into the two Parallel Distributed Processing books, written by a group at UC San Diego.**
- **Parallel** means many neurons calculate their activations at the same time.
- **Distributed** means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons.
- By 1986, forward propagation and backpropagation were well worked out. One contributor, **Geoffrey Hinton**, later won the **2024 Nobel Prize in Physics** for this work.

- **Speech changes all the time**, because every small moment has new formants.
- **Language also changes over time**, because a sentence is many words, one after another.

notes_v10_1: - **AI systems are built in levels, and each level is made of the level below it.**

- **A single neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number.** It multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results, which is the **inner product**. The symbol **sigma** means add them up. This simple multiplying and adding models the electrochemical activity of a real neuron.

- **A neural network takes in one vector and gives back a whole vector of decisions.** Its layers are connected by sets of weights. Each set of weights turns one vector into the next vector through many inner products.

- **A large language model takes in many vectors, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision about what comes next.** Picture 15 vectors, each one standing for one word of a sentence. The job of the model is to **predict the sixteenth**.

- In real systems, there are hundreds of thousands to a million input vectors, and this set is called the **context window**. Each vector is also thousands of numbers long, which is why huge data centers are needed.
- The sixteenth vector is a **probability distribution over the next word**. English has about 30,000 words, and each entry gives the chance that one particular word comes next.

- **A large language model is made of neural networks, and its knowledge is still in its weights.** Each set of weights is a **layer**, and real systems have about a hundred or more layers. An LLM's knowledge of how to write an essay is stored in its weights.
- **An LLM is a dynamical system, which is why the Nobel Prize for AI was given in physics.**
- A mass-spring system starts from **initial conditions**, and the rule decides what happens next.
- An LLM's initial condition is its set of input vectors. Each layer turns those vectors into **better vectors**, step after step, until the last layer can predict the next word.
- The calculation at every step is the **inner product**, repeated billions or trillions of times.

title: Heads, layers and the LLM as a dynamical system

heads.opening: **An LLM is built from layers, and each layer contains several attention heads working side by side.** A **head** is a set of weights that handles one kind of relationship in the input. Layers go one after another from the input to the output.
heads.mechanism: Each layer combines what its heads found into improved vectors and passes them on. The next layer then works on vectors that already include those relationships. So heads give the model width, and layers give it depth.
heads.consequence: So a head is a part inside one LLM, **not a separate person or agent**. Calling a head an expert does not promise it has a skill people can name. Several heads in one layer are not the same as several whole agents sending messages.

dynamic-depth.opening: **A dynamical system takes a state and changes it again and again by a rule.** An oscillator updates its position and velocity over time. A layered LLM updates its vectors layer by layer through its depth.
dynamic-depth.mechanism: Following one value through the layers shows how the vectors change. Each layer has its own learned weights, so the comparison is about **repeated change**, not the same rule at every layer.
dynamic-depth.consequence: So in both systems, **the output of one step becomes the input to the next**. The comparison does not mean an LLM layer is a physical spring.

notes_v10_1: - **Predicting the next word is so hard that an LLM needs many layers, and many parallel heads inside each layer.** A **head** is one expert. In each layer, the knowledge from all the heads is combined to make **improved vectors**. Then the next layer does the same thing again.
- **This is a question for the exam.** **Layers go one after another from the input to the output. Heads sit side by side inside each layer.**
- **A classroom comparison explains heads and layers.** Imagine trying to improve yourself by visiting a series of classes, one class after another.
- In each class, every student gives you their own opinion on how to improve. Each student is like a **head**.
- You then **combine** all of those opinions into one improved version of yourself. Combining the heads' opinions is what a layer does.
- Then you go to the next class and do the same thing again. **The classes are the layers.**
- Layers give an LLM depth, which is one round of improvement after another. Heads give it width, which is many experts asked at the same time within each round.

- **Each head is a set of weights, and every head learns.** An expert's knowledge is in its weights. Every head in every layer learns how to improve the vectors so that the last layer can predict the next word.
- Large systems have **a hundred or more layers** and about **a hundred heads** in each layer. That shows how complicated language, vision and the other tasks really are.

- The heads and layers are trained like everything else. A sentence such as "the dog that ... barks" is taken from text, and the system predicts the next word. software.opening: **Software 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 are three ways to build a program.** In Software 1.0, a person writes the steps. In Software 2.0, a network learns its weights from examples. In Software 3.0, an agentic system of LLMs builds the program from plain English instructions.
software.mechanism: A Software 1.0 program spells out each operation in a language such as Python. A trained network stores what it learned about inputs and outputs in its weights. In Software 3.0, LLMs can draft, check and revise the result, and doing this from plain English is called **vibe coding**.
software.consequence: So the three **can work together in one system** instead of replacing each other. The agents still rely on trained weights and on programs that run.

notes_v10_1: - **An LLM that learns English syllables can be built by describing it in plain English to an agentic system.** The request specified **five layers**, **four heads in each layer**, and **input vectors that are 64 numbers long**.

- The request asked the system to pick **1000 English words at random** and train the LLM on them. Training meant taking each letter, trying to **predict the next letter**, and then improving the weights to predict better.
- The request also asked the system to show **ten generated words after each step of training**, to reveal what the LLM knew about English at that point.

- **The agentic system translated the request into its own technical terms.** It built a small **character-level transformer**, which is another name for an LLM that works one letter at a time, with **attention heads**.
- **Attention** means a head looks over the rest of the sequence to decide which preceding items matter, the same way predicting barks requires paying attention to dog.
- The system chose to train on **pronunciations** instead of spellings, so the silent e in shave would not mislead it. It also wrote the program in Python on its own.

- **The results show how hard the problem is.** After training on 1000 words, the generated words were **still mostly gibberish**, with perhaps a few vowels starting to appear in the right places. The suggested next step was to train on **10,000 words** for many more steps. Deciding which sounds can follow which seems easy for any speaker, but it is not easy even for an LLM.

- **Software 2.0** is giving a neural network input data and output data, so the program becomes the network's **weights**.

- **Software 3.0** is using an agentic system, a set of LLMs talking to each other and to the user, to build and run a program. Doing this with plain English instructions is called **vibe coding**. It means someone with a good idea no longer needs to hire a programmer to build it.

- That paper started **information theory**, one of the most important fields in engineering. Information theory is still important for LLMs today.
- **Viterbi**, one of the developers of dynamic programming, published his most famous work in an information theory journal. So the ideas behind backpropagation and LLMs share the same roots.

- It asked the system to pick **1000 English words at random** and train the LLM on them. Training meant taking each letter, trying to **predict the next letter**, and then improving the weights to predict better.
- It also asked the system to show **ten generated words after each step of training**, to reveal what the LLM knew about English at that point.

- The agentic system translated the request into its own technical terms. It built a small **character-level transformer**, which is another name for an LLM that works one letter at a time, with **attention heads**.
- **Attention** means a head looks over the rest of the sequence to decide which items before it matter. This is the same way predicting barks requires paying attention to dog.
- The system chose to train on **pronunciations** instead of spellings, so the silent e in shave would not confuse it. It also wrote the program in Python on its own.

- The results show how hard the problem is. After training on 1000 words, the generated words were **still mostly gibberish**, with maybe a few vowels starting to show up in the right places. The suggested next step was to train on **10,000 words** for many more steps.
- Deciding which sounds can follow which seems easy for any speaker, but it is not easy even for an LLM.
- This way of working has a name.
- **Software 1.0** is writing programs in a programming language such as Python or C.
- **Software 2.0** is giving a neural network input data and output data, so the program becomes the network's **weights**, which predict the outputs from the inputs.

- **Software 3.0** is using an agentic system, which is a set of LLMs talking to each other and to the user, to build and run a program. Doing this with plain English instructions is called **vibe coding**. It means someone with a good idea no longer needs to hire a programmer to build it.

- The first attempt at this kind of problem was **Claude Shannon's 1948 paper, "A Mathematical Theory of Communication."** Shannon worked by hand and produced sequences of letters that got closer and closer to English. They went from random strings of consonants, to strings with vowels, to strings with real short words.
- That paper started **information theory**, one of the most important fields in engineering. Information theory is still important for LLMs today.
- **Viterbi**, one of the people who developed dynamic programming, published his most famous work in an information theory journal. So the ideas behind backpropagation and LLMs share the same roots.

title: Phonotactics and guessing the next letter

phonotactics.opening: **Phonotactics is the set of rules for which sound sequences a language allows.** English allows some consonant clusters before or after a vowel. It rules out others in the same position, so flat is a word but lfat is not.
phonotactics.mechanism: An **onset** comes before the vowel of a syllable, as in split. A **coda** comes after it, as in lamp. A cluster that works across a syllable break may not work at the start of a syllable. So Atlantic is fine, because t and l sit in different syllables, but tlantic is impossible.
phonotactics.consequence: So **the rules are about sounds, not letters**. Knee is spelled with a k, but its normal pronunciation does not begin with /k/.

letter-guess.opening: **Guessing the next letter of a word shows what you know about English word patterns.** After sp at the start of a word, l, r or a vowel can come next. The letter n cannot come next, because it does not fit the English onset pattern.
letter-guess.mechanism: Some beginnings allow many next letters, and others allow only a few. A probability distribution shows this by **spreading out** after ra and **piling up** on a few vowels after skr.
letter-guess.consequence: So a network that learns from many completions can pick up these patterns **without being told each rule**. The spelling game tests real language knowledge, but it is not a full description of English sounds.

notes_v10_1: - **English allows only certain sequences of sounds in its words, and every speaker knows which sequences are allowed.** **A simple English syllable is a consonant, then a vowel, then a consonant**, as in Don, mat, sit, cup, dog and fish.
- The pattern is about **sounds, not letters**. The silent e in shave, kite and rope does not count. Two letters can spell one consonant sound, as in ship, chin and bath.

- **Syllables can also have clusters, and only some clusters are allowed.** A **cluster** is a group of consonants together. A cluster before the vowel is an **onset**, as in split, flat and black. A cluster after the vowel is a **coda**, as in desk, help and lamp.

- Each real word has an impossible twin marked with a star, such as **flat** and **lfat**, **help** and **hepl**, and **lamp** and **lapm**. Many twins use the same letters in a different order, so the order matters.

- **The order is a mirror image around the vowel.** In flat, the l is right next to the vowel and the f is farther out. In help, the l is again right next to the vowel, now on the other side, and the p is farther out. Each impossible twin puts the wrong consonant next to the vowel.
- A made-up product name like "desb" or "lapm" sounds un-English right away, because it breaks these rules.
- **A long word is a chain of syllables, and each syllable follows the same rules.** Examples are ba-na-na, At-lan-tic and ath-lete.
- The sounds t and l are fine across a syllable break, but **tl cannot start a syllable**. That is why Atlantic is a word but tlantic is impossible.
- The sound **ng** can end a syllable, as in ring, but it can never start one.
- So whether a sequence of sounds is allowed depends on where the syllable breaks are.
- **Every language has its own sequence rules.**
- Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable.
- Cantonese also allows a final p, as in cup.
- Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, which English never allows.
- Spanish speakers change a word like stadium so that it starts with e, because Spanish does not allow s and t together at the start of a word.

People agree on their guesses quickly, and how much they agree changes from item to item.
- **After a vowel, almost any letter can come next.** After "ra," likely letters include t, n, r and l, and many other letters are possible too.
- **At the start of a word, the choices narrow to exactly what an English onset allows.**
- After **sp**, the next letter is l, r or a vowel, and never n.
- After **k**, the next letter is a vowel or n, as in knee, and never t.
- After **b** and **f**, the next letter is r, l or a vowel, and never n.
- After **sh**, the next letter is a vowel or r, as in shrimp.
- After **skr**, or after **m** at the start of a word, only a vowel can come.
- After **bram**, the letter b is almost certain, as in bramble, though a new syllable could also start there.

- **Guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item, which is the same game an LLM plays.** A GPT trained only on this game learns English sounds and spelling, because its predictions can only improve by matching the patterns of English syllables.
- The GPT's prediction is a **probability distribution** over the next letter, and the shape of that distribution holds the knowledge.
- After "ra," the distribution is **flat**, spread over many letters. After "skr," it is **sharply peaked** on a few vowels, because English allows nothing else there.
- The more the letters so far limit what can come next, the more the probability piles onto a few letters.
